records.title: TikTok Content Sharing Guidelines (Direct Post API)
records.summary: TikTok's developer rules for the Content Posting API's Direct Post: what an unaudited client may do, the daily caps, the audit's intended-use test and the UX a posting app must show.
records.why_it_matters: This page decides whether a one-person pipeline can publish to TikTok publicly at all. Without an audit every post is private, and the audit does not accept a tool for your own accounts.
records.fit_notes: For one developer posting to their own account this is a dead end for public posts: unaudited clients post SELF_ONLY, and the audit's 'Not acceptable' list names a utility tool for accounts you or your team manage. Posts can be made public later by hand in the app. Self-hosted schedulers (Postiz, Mixpost Pro) need their own TikTok app and hit the same wall; a hosted scheduler with an audited app is the remaining official route, not checked here. Unaudited clients are also limited to 5 posting users per 24 hours. The page bans watermarks or promo text on shared content. Page last updated August 4, 2026.

related.note: A self-hosted Postiz needs its own TikTok app, which this audit rule leaves private-only for own-account use.

claims.text: Without an audit, every Direct Post upload is private-only; an audit lifts it.
claims.quote: As a developer, you can use this API in an unverified status, but all content uploaded via this endpoint will be restricted to private viewing mode. To lift this restriction, your API client must undergo an audit to verify compliance with our Terms of Service.
claims.locator: Direct Post API - Developer Guidelines, first paragraph

claims.text: The audit rejects a tool that only uploads to accounts you or your team manage, which is the single-developer case.
claims.quote: Not acceptable: A utility tool to help upload contents to the account(s) you or your team manages. ❌

claims.text: Each creator account has a cap of about 15 Direct Posts a day, shared across every app that posts for it.
claims.quote: The upper limit may vary among creators (typically around 15 posts per day/ creator account) and is shared across all API Clients using Direct Post.
claims.locator: Direct Post API - Developer Guidelines, Posting cap

checked.what: visible page text (last updated August 4, 2026) against the earlier scan's two quotes; both found verbatim

records.title: TikTok Content Posting API - Direct Post reference
records.summary: The request and response reference for TikTok's /v2/post/publish/video/init/ endpoint: post_info fields, source types, error codes and the per-token rate limit.
records.why_it_matters: It holds the AI-label flag an agent should set on generated video and the error an unaudited client gets when the account is public.
records.fit_notes: Set post_info.is_aigc=true on generated clips; the page says it adds the 'Creator labeled as AI-generated' tag. The error unaudited_client_can_only_post_to_private_accounts means an unaudited client also needs the account itself set to private, not only the post. 6 init requests per minute per user token is not a constraint at 15 posts a day, but a retry loop can hit it. Rate limits for other endpoints are on a separate page (600 per minute for user/info, video/list), not made a record.

claims.text: Setting is_aigc marks the post with TikTok's creator AI-generated label.
claims.quote: Set to true if the video is AI generated content. If set, the video will be labelled with Creator labeled as AI-generated tag in video's description.

claims.text: An unaudited client is blocked at init when the target account is not private.
claims.quote: Unaudited clients can only post to a private account. The publish attempt will be blocked when calling /publish/video/init/.

claims.text: The init endpoint allows 6 requests per minute per user access token.
claims.quote: Note: Each user access_token is limited to 6 requests per minute.

checked.what: visible reference text against the claims

records.title: TikTok Content Posting API - Media Transfer Guide
records.summary: TikTok's rules for sending the file: chunked FILE_UPLOAD sizes, PULL_FROM_URL with a verified domain or URL prefix, and the accepted video formats, frame rates, resolution, length and size.
records.why_it_matters: These are the encode targets for a clip an agent renders for TikTok, from TikTok's own API page rather than a creator blog.
records.fit_notes: Render H.264 MP4 at 23-60 fps, 360-4096 px per side, at most 4 GB. The API accepts up to 10 minutes, but the account's own cap (3, 5 or 10 minutes) applies and creator_info returns it as max_video_post_duration_sec. Chunks must be 5-64 MB (the final chunk up to 128 MB), files under 5 MB go in one piece. PULL_FROM_URL needs a domain or URL prefix verified in the TikTok developer portal, so a laptop pipeline usually uses FILE_UPLOAD.

claims.text: TikTok accepts MP4, WebM or MOV in H.264, H.265, VP8 or VP9, at 23 to 60 fps.
claims.quote:
Framerate restrictions

Minimum of 23 FPS

Maximum of 60 FPS

claims.text: The API takes videos up to 10 minutes; the creator's own maximum may be shorter and TikTok users may trim.
claims.quote: The longest video a developer can send via the initialize Upload Video endpoint is 10 minutes. TikTok users may trim developer-sent videos inside the TikTok app to fit their accounts' actual maximum publish durations.

claims.text: Upload chunks must be between 5 MB and 64 MB, and the final chunk may be up to 128 MB; a video under 5 MB is uploaded whole as one chunk.
claims.quote: Each chunk must be at least 5 MB but no greater than 64 MB, except for the final chunk, which can be greater than chunk_size (up to 128 MB) to accommodate any trailing bytes.

records.title: TikTok Community Guidelines - Integrity and Authenticity (Edited Media and AIGC)
records.summary: TikTok's community guideline on misinformation, edited media and AI-generated content, including the creator labelling duty.
records.why_it_matters: It states when a generated clip must carry the AI label and what happens to unlabelled realistic AI content.
records.fit_notes: The duty covers realistic-looking scenes or people; a clearly stylised motion-graphics clip is not named. Via the API the label is post_info.is_aigc on the Direct Post record. The URL redirects to www.tiktok.com/safety/en/policies-and-engagement/integrity-authenticity. TikTok's support page on AI labels (support.tiktok.com) rendered empty here and was not read.

related.note: is_aigc is the API form of this label.

claims.text: TikTok requires creators to label AI-generated or heavily edited content that shows realistic scenes or people, and may remove, restrict or label it if they do not.
claims.quote: we require creators to label AI-generated or significantly edited content that shows realistic-looking scenes or people. Unlabeled content may be removed, restricted, or labeled by our team, depending on the harm it could cause.

claims.text: A label does not make misleading content on matters of public importance acceptable.
claims.quote: Even with labels, some edited or AI-generated content can still be harmful. We don’t allow content that’s misleading about matters of public importance or harmful to individuals.

checked.what: visible policy text after redirect to the safety policies page

records.title: YouTube Data API (v3) revision history
records.summary: Google's change log for the YouTube Data API v3. Two entries matter here: November 2, 2026, which ends private-only uploads for unverified projects, and October 30, 2024, which adds the synthetic-media flag.
records.why_it_matters: Most guides still say an unaudited YouTube project uploads private-only. Since November 2, 2026 that is no longer true, which makes YouTube the easiest public target for a one-person pipeline.
records.fit_notes: The 2020 private-only rule is still on the same page under July 28, 2020; read the date. Set status.privacyStatus explicitly: the default is now public, and a test upload you meant to keep private goes live. Set status.containsSyntheticMedia=true on realistic generated clips (see the disclosure help page). The page URL now redirects to developers.google.com/youtube/data/revision_history. The quota (100 uploads a day) is on the videos.insert record.

claims.text: Since November 2, 2026, videos uploaded from unverified API projects are no longer forced private, reversing the July 2020 rule.
claims.quote: Videos uploaded through the videos.insert method from unverified API projects are no longer restricted to private viewing mode. This change reverses the policy announced on July 28, 2020, which restricted videos uploaded from unverified API projects created after that date to private viewing mode until the project completed an audit.

claims.text: An upload without status.privacyStatus now defaults to public.
claims.quote: If you don't specify a value for the status.privacyStatus property in a videos.insert request, the uploaded video's privacy status defaults to public.

claims.text: The API flag for realistic altered or synthetic content is status.containsSyntheticMedia, settable on insert or update.
claims.quote: To indicate whether a video contains A/S content, set the status.containsSyntheticMedia property. This property can be set when calling the videos.insert or videos.update methods.

checked.what: visible page text, entries November 2, 2026, October 30, 2024 and July 28, 2020, against the earlier scan's claim; confirmed

records.title: YouTube Data API - videos.insert and quota costs
records.summary: The reference for uploading a video through the YouTube Data API, read together with the quota cost page.

Quotas reset at midnight Pacific Time. Files up to 256 GB, any video/* type. Needs a Google Cloud project and OAuth consent for your own channel; no cost stated. Both pages redirect to developers.google.com/youtube/data/...

claims.quote: Quota impact: 100 calls per day. A call to this method has a quota cost of 1 unit in the Video Uploads quota bucket.

claims.text: A project gets 100 search.list calls, 100 videos.insert calls and 10,000 units for all other endpoints per day.
claims.quote: Projects that enable the YouTube Data API have a default quota allocation of 100 search.list calls, 100 videos.insert calls, and 10,000 units per day combined for all other endpoints.

claims.text: Uploads may be up to 256 GB of any video MIME type.
claims.quote:
Maximum file size: 256GB

records.title: YouTube channel monetization policies (inauthentic content)
records.summary: YouTube's Partner Program policy page. Its inauthentic-content section, renamed from 'repetitious content' on July 15, 2025, sets the bar for AI-assisted and templated channels.
records.why_it_matters: An agent pipeline that makes many similar clips is the exact pattern this policy names, so it decides whether the channel can earn.
records.fit_notes: AI use is allowed and named as monetisable when it serves your own narrative; templated, interchangeable videos are not. Reused-content review applies to the whole channel, so a run of near-identical generated Shorts can cost monetisation on everything. Separate rule: AI personas giving health, legal, finance or political advice cannot monetise. Policy text, not a measured threshold; reviewers judge.

claims.text: Monetised content must not be mass-produced, generic or repetitive.
claims.quote: Not be mass-produced, generic, repetitive, or manipulative. It should be made for the enjoyment or education of viewers, rather than for the sole purpose of getting views.

claims.text: AI content from generic templates that looks mass-produced, without the creator's own insight, is a named example of inauthentic content.
claims.quote: AI-generated content made with generic or unoriginal templates giving the impression of mass production without adding the creator’s original, authentic insights or perspective

claims.text: Using AI to visualise a character and story you invented is a named example of content that can monetise.
claims.quote: Content that expresses your unique creative voice, like using AI to visualize a unique character and narrative you invented
claims.locator: Examples of what is allowed to monetize

checked.what: visible help page text (hl=en) against the 'mass production' wording from the earlier scan

records.title: YouTube Help - Disclosing use of GenAI content
records.summary: YouTube's rule on when creators must disclose AI-generated or altered content, how the label shows, and when YouTube applies it automatically, including from C2PA metadata.
records.why_it_matters: It is the only first-party page read here that says a platform reads C2PA, and it says a C2PA-triggered label cannot be removed.
records.fit_notes: Disclosure is needed for realistic content and AI music, not for clearly fantastical or animated content or for script, caption and thumbnail help. Repeated non-disclosure can lead to removal or YPP suspension. If your generator embeds C2PA, expect a label you cannot turn off. The API equivalent is status.containsSyntheticMedia (revision history record). Title read here: 'Disclosing use of GenAI content'.

claims.text: Creators must disclose realistic AI-generated or altered content.
claims.quote: We require creators to disclose AI-generated or altered content that seems realistic.
claims.locator: Disclosing use of GenAI content, intro

claims.text: YouTube may label content automatically when it carries C2PA metadata, and that label cannot be changed by the creator.
claims.quote: However, content made with YouTube’s AI tools, content containing C2PA metadata, or content labeled after manual review can not be adjusted.

claims.text: Repeated failure to disclose can bring a forced label, removal or YouTube Partner Program suspension.
claims.quote: Creators who consistently choose not to disclose this information may be subject to manual application of a label, or penalties from YouTube, including removal of content or suspension from the YouTube Partner Program.

records.title: YouTube Help - Understand three-minute YouTube Shorts
records.summary: YouTube's page on which uploads count as Shorts: square or vertical video up to three minutes uploaded on or after 2024-10-15 (2025-12-08 for Official Artist Channels), with a copyright rule for Shorts over one minute.
records.why_it_matters: It tells an agent the aspect ratio and length that make an upload count as a Short.
records.fit_notes: Shorts classification is automatic from aspect ratio, length and upload date (with a later cutoff for Official Artist Channels), so the API upload needs no Shorts flag. A Short over one minute with any active copyright claim is blocked worldwide, so generated music must be clean. No resolution or bitrate figures on this page.

claims.text: A Short over one minute with an active copyright claim is blocked globally.
claims.quote: Any Short that is over one minute in duration with an active copyright claim of any type, including manual claims, will be blocked globally on YouTube.

records.title: C2PA FAQs (Content Credentials)
records.summary: The C2PA's own FAQ on Content Credentials: what a C2PA manifest is, how it is signed, and how a product gets a trusted signing certificate.
records.why_it_matters: YouTube states it labels content with C2PA metadata as AI and does not let the creator undo it, so a pipeline should know whether its generator embeds a manifest.
records.fit_notes: A manifest trusted under the official C2PA Trust List is signed with a certificate that only products in the C2PA Conformance Program receive; legacy ITL certificates still validate in tools that use the ITL, but validators need not respect them. In practice the manifest comes from the generator or editor; check whether yours embeds one and whether your ffmpeg step keeps it. Only YouTube's own page was found here stating it reads C2PA; Meta's labelling pages did not render. The spec itself was not read.

related.note: YouTube applies a fixed AI label to C2PA content.

claims.text: A Content Credential, or C2PA manifest, is digitally signed and hashes the asset, so edits break the link.
claims.quote: Consumers can trust that C2PA data was captured correctly because each Content Credential (also known as a C2PA Manifest) is digitally signed by a trusted implementation.
claims.locator: How can consumers of C2PA data be assured the data was captured correctly?

claims.text: The specification can be implemented without joining, but a Claim Signing Certificate and a place on the Conforming Products List require the Conformance Program.
claims.quote: However, to receive a Claim Signing Certificate and be listed on the official Conforming Products List, your product must undergo evaluation and legal onboarding through the C2PA Conformance Program.
claims.locator: Do I need to join C2PA to implement the specification?

checked.what: independent fact-check: claims, prose and category fields against the saved source
